title: Black-Box Hypothesis
formal:
Is every semantic property of Boolean functions that is decidable in randomized polynomial time from a circuit description also decidable in randomized polynomial time from only input-output queries and a circuit-size bound?

More precisely, for every family of total predicates \(F_n:\{0,1\}^{2^n}\to\{0,1\}\), does
\[F\in\mathrm{wbBPP}\ \Longrightarrow\ F\in\mathrm{bbBPP}\]
hold under the definitions below? The reverse implication follows from polynomial-time circuit evaluation, so this is the usual equality formulation of the Black-Box Hypothesis. The property is defined on every truth table, and a white-box algorithm must be correct for every circuit description of that truth table.

source_formulation.text: The main statement, which we will call here ‘the Black-Box Hypothesis’, remains open.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 4

why: The hypothesis asks whether reading an efficient program can reveal any efficiently decidable fact about its function that could not also be learned efficiently by running the function on selected inputs. It connects the limits of program analysis with circuit complexity and obfuscation. Its truth would imply that NP is not contained in BPP, while restricted failures have known consequences for the complexity of circuit satisfiability.

sentences: The Black-Box Hypothesis compares access to a Boolean circuit’s code with access to its input-output behavior.
It concerns total semantic properties that a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm decides correctly on every circuit representation.
The proposed black-box algorithm receives unary input length and circuit-size bounds and may make adaptive evaluations of the function.
Its total running time, including queries, must be polynomial in those bounds with error at most one third on each input.
Known restricted-model results and promise-property counterexamples do not settle this general hypothesis.

definitions:
For each integer \(n\ge0\), a Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) has the length-\(2^n\) truth table \(\operatorname{tt}(f)\), ordered lexicographically by input. A property is an arbitrary family \(F=(F_n)_{n\ge0}\) of total Boolean predicates on these tables. It need not be invariant under permutations of the input variables or table positions. Its semantic character means that two circuits computing the same \(n\)-input function have the same required property value.

A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with designated input vertices \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), constants \(0,1\), binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates and one designated output. Wires may share gate outputs; unrestricted depth is allowed. Unused designated input vertices are retained. Its size \(s(C)\) is the number of vertices plus wires, and its computed function is \(f_C\). Define \(s(f)=\min\{s(C):f_C=f\}\). Counting input vertices is a harmless explicit convention because the black-box resource bound includes \(n\).

Descriptions list all vertices in topological order, their types and earlier incoming indices, followed by the output index; integers use self-delimiting binary fields. This gives a polynomial-time parsable encoding of length polynomial in \(s(C)+1\), including all \(n\) input vertices. Any fixed encoding with these properties gives the same polynomial-time target. Malformed descriptions are rejected.

A property belongs to \(\mathrm{wbBPP}\) if there are one uniform probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(c,k\) such that \(A\) halts on every input and every random-bit sequence within \(c(N+1)^k\) steps, where \(N\) is description length, and
\[\forall C,\qquad \Pr[A(\operatorname{desc}(C))=F_n(\operatorname{tt}(f_C))]\ge2/3.\]
The same machine must work across all sizes and arities and on every representation of a function, including padded or redundant circuits. The acceptance probabilities for different representations need not be equal; each must give the correct Boolean property value with the stated error bound.

A property belongs to \(\mathrm{bbBPP}\) if there are one uniform probabilistic oracle Turing machine \(B\) and fixed positive integers \(d,\ell\) such that \(B^f(1^n,1^m)\) halts within \(d(n+m+1)^\ell\) steps on every random-bit sequence, and
\[\forall n\ge0\ \forall f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\ \forall m\ge1,\quad m\ge s(f)\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[B^f(1^n,1^m)=F_n(\operatorname{tt}(f))]\ge2/3.\]
Here \(m\) is an integer upper bound, not necessarily the minimum circuit size. Both parameters are in unary. A query consists of an explicitly written \(n\)-bit string \(x\); the oracle returns \(f(x)\) in one step. Writing and manipulating the query counts toward time. Invalid-length queries return a fixed zero bit. Queries may be adaptive, and all computation between queries also counts. Thus the bound is on running time, not merely the number of oracle calls. The same machine and polynomial work for all valid bounds \(m\). If \(m<s(f)\), no correctness is required, but the running-time bound remains.

Both machines use independent fair random bits, and all probabilities above are over those bits for each fixed input or oracle. They have no advice or other oracle. In the black-box case, \(f\) and the unary parameters are the only supplied information about the function; no circuit, truth table, distribution on circuits or special representation is given. The circuit-size promise in this definition does not turn \(F_n\) into a partial property: \(F_n\) is defined on every Boolean function.

The quantifiers allow \(A,B\) and their polynomial constants to depend on \(F\). The conclusion is existence of a suitable \(B\) for every white-box decidable property, not an additional requirement of an effective procedure that transforms arbitrary machine descriptions into black-box algorithms.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the universal implication. A proof must establish a uniform black-box algorithm with the stated total running-time and pointwise error guarantees for every total semantic property in white-box BPP. A refutation must specify one such property and a correct white-box BPP algorithm and prove that no black-box BPP algorithm decides it under the supplied-size-bound model. A property defined only on a promised family of circuits, a distinction between two encodings of the same function, or a lower bound only for nonadaptive queries does not alone meet this criterion.

context_blocks.text: The 2017 source identifies this as the total-property form of the scaled-down Rice’s theorem conjecture originating in work on program obfuscation. It distinguishes the still-open hypothesis from conditional counterexamples to a promise version; those counterexamples do not decide a property on every circuit.

The authors prove consequences of particular kinds of hypothetical counterexamples, including ones with highly sensitive low-complexity functions. These are conditional implications for circuit satisfiability, rather than a general proof or disproof of the hypothesis.

The 2021 paper retains the original hypothesis as open and studies other combinations of analysts and represented computations. Its positive results for restricted circuit analysts, and its equivalence involving nondeterministic circuits as boxes, change the computational models and do not settle ordinary circuits with uniform BPP analysts.

The cost of black-box computation includes the unary circuit-size bound. This avoids demanding a polynomial-in-arity algorithm for properties of functions whose smallest circuits are already exponentially large, and makes the two kinds of access comparable.
